newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar dives, rates soar as investors pull plug.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar dives, rates soar as investors pull plug.

text.p: Long-term investors in New Zealand assets on Friday pulled the plug on their positions, causing the kiwi dollar to plunge over one U.S. cent and short-term interest rates to rocket skyward.
The New Zealand currency closed at 65 U.S. cents, down from US$0.6600/07 at Thursday's close, while the key 90-day bank bill rate spiked up 90 basis points to 8.60 percent.
Dealers said the kiwi dollar faced further falls, despite the increasing attractiveness of higher rates of return on New Zealand assets that accompanied rising interest rates.
"It's fine to get the extra two or three percent on your investment, but what happens if the currency goes down three big figures ?" said a bank chief dealer.
"People won't get into it while there's a perception that the exchange rate will go lower -- it just isn't worth it.
"At the end of the day I think it's just a general disinvestment, which means interest rates are really irrelevant to the equation."
Rates rose to offset the impact of the Kiwi's fall on monetary conditions.
Unlike other central banks, New Zealand's Reserve Bank has no key interest rate mechanism with which to steer short-term monetary conditions.
It relies instead on a formula called the Monetary Conditions Index (MCI), which measures conditions by bringing together the New Zealand dollar and the 90-day bank bill rate.
The MCI opened over 100 points below the RBNZ's desired level, prompting fears of intervention from the bank.
But the money market's response to the sagging currency was an almost flawless rebalancing act, the MCI closing the session in touch with the Reserve Bank's desired levels.
However, this level of short-term interest rate clearly threatens to knock-on to mortgage rates, bankers say.
New Zealand variable home loan rates currently cluster around 8.95 percent with some as low as 8.20 percent.
On Friday one major home lender, Countrywide Bank, repeated that it expected to have to raise its variable mortgage unless there was a major reversal in short bill rates was imminent.

Like others in the market, Countrywide criticised policy makers for setting the preconditions which were now placing upward pressure on rates at a time when the economy is in a low growth phase and showing extremely low inflation trends.
And if the currency continues to fall and rates keep rising, analysts say an upturn in economic activity hoped for by the government may be stiffled.

HSBC said in a market commentary: "With the appearance of being a managed currency, the New Zealand dollar is vulnerable to attack from offshore speculators, and creating the very real possibility that 90-day rates can be pushed into double digits, and choking off economic growth in the foreseeable future".

During this week there has been a growing awareness in the New Zealand market that some international traders are looking at the Kiwi dollar in the same light as the South-East Asian currencies which have been attacked in recent weeks.
The Australian Financial Review newspaper reported on Friday the kiwi appeared to have emerged as a new target for the powerful hedge funds, often U.S.-based.
It quoted John Noonan, head of international sales for National Australia Bank in Singapore, as saying problems facing Asian currencies were having a ripple effect through the region.
"Every currency in the region has been put under the microscope and New Zealand is under a bit of pressure at the moment," he said.
